content: Folliculitis refers to the inflammation of one or more hair follicles, which can occur on any part of the skin. It is classified based on the depth of involvement (superficial or deep), the underlying cause (infectious or non-infectious), and the chronicity of the condition (acute or chronic/recurrent). Non-infectious forms of folliculitis include conditions such as pseudofolliculitis barbae, eosinophilic folliculitis, drug-induced acneiform folliculitis, folliculitis decalvans, and acne keloidalis nuchae. The pathophysiology of folliculitis depends on the causative agent. It may result from bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic infections, or from non-infectious factors such as follicular trauma, inflammation, occlusion, or the use of topical steroids. Eosinophilic folliculitis, although of unknown cause, has been linked to microorganisms like Demodex mites, Pityrosporum yeast, and bacteria, as well as potential autoimmune processes. Microscopically, superficial folliculitis is characterized by neutrophilic infiltration confined to the infundibulum of the hair follicle, while deep folliculitis involves the deeper follicle and dermis. Chronic cases may show granulomatous inflammation with giant cells containing keratin and fragmented hair. Suppurative folliculitis often resolves spontaneously, but longstanding cases may lead to granuloma formation, fibrosis, or scarring. Folliculitis must be differentiated from other conditions such as acne vulgaris, rosacea, periorofacial dermatitis, acneiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa, transient acantholytic dermatosis, insect bites, papular urticaria, milia, and contact dermatitis. Superficial folliculitis is common, but its exact incidence is unknown as many affected individuals do not seek medical attention. It can occur in all age groups, though certain types, such as hot tub folliculitis and Demodex folliculitis, are more common in adults. There is no gender predilection for superficial folliculitis, but males are more frequently affected by herpes folliculitis and pityrosporum folliculitis. Eosinophilic folliculitis is often seen in HIV-infected individuals. Racially, pseudofolliculitis barbae predominantly affects individuals of African descent. The most common cause of folliculitis is Staphylococcus aureus, which infects damaged hair follicles. Damage may result from friction, shaving, or follicular blockage. Other causes include fungal infections (e.g., Tinea barbae caused by Trichophyton rubrum), pseudomonas infections (e.g., hot tub folliculitis), and drug side effects. Specific conditions like pseudofolliculitis barbae occur when curly beard hairs re-enter the skin, causing inflammation.g., smallpox and anthrax). Most cases of folliculitis are asymptomatic, but some may present with itchy, painful, or burning red papules or pustules around hair follicles. If untreated, folliculitis can progress to furuncles or carbuncles, which may rupture and discharge pus. Complications include cellulitis, scarring, sinus tract formation, permanent hair loss, and recurrence. In individuals with darker skin, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation may occur and take months to years to resolve. Prognosis is excellent with accurate diagnosis and treatment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination. Symptoms include clusters of small red bumps or white-headed pimples around hair follicles, itchy or painful skin lesions, and pus-filled blisters that may crust over. Physical examination may reveal erythematous papules and pustules, with superficial folliculitis presenting as small lesions on an erythematous base and deep folliculitis as tender plaques or nodules with scarring. Systemic symptoms like fever may occur in deeper infections or immunocompromised patients. Laboratory tests are generally reserved for resistant or recurrent cases. These may include complete blood count (CBC) showing leukocytosis or eosinophilia, HIV testing for eosinophilic folliculitis, and bacterial cultures for suspected infections. Fungal infections can be diagnosed with KOH preparation or fungal culture, while viral folliculitis may require PCR or immunofluorescence testing. Skin biopsy and histology can confirm the diagnosis and identify the causative agent. Treatment of folliculitis depends on the underlying cause. Uncomplicated bacterial folliculitis is treated with topical antibiotics like mupirocin or clindamycin, while recurrent or resistant cases may require oral antibiotics. Pseudomonas folliculitis may be treated with oral ciprofloxacin in immunocompromised patients. Gram-negative folliculitis, often caused by prolonged antibiotic use, is managed by discontinuing the implicated antibiotic and using trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Eosinophilic folliculitis responds to indomethacin, PUVA therapy, topical tacrolimus, or isotretinoin. Fungal folliculitis is treated with oral antifungals like fluconazole or itraconazole, and viral folliculitis with antivirals such as valacyclovir or acyclovir. Demodex folliculitis may require antiparasitic agents like permethrin or oral ivermectin. Surgical intervention may be necessary for severe cases of folliculitis keloidalis that are resistant to medical therapy, larger than 3 cm, or associated with fibrotic plaques or nodules. A decolonization regimen with topical mupirocin and chlorhexidine body washes may be used in recurrent cases. Follow-up after two weeks is recommended to assess treatment response.
